To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the follicular B cell population in the lungs of tuberculosis-infected animals differs from classical B2 cells in phenotype and functional activity.

during the course of tuberculosis in the lung B lymphocytes form follicle-like structures and produce IL-6 and -11, but no type 1 and no anti-inflammatory cytokines, thus having no protective role in tuberculosis.

(1) during the course of experimental tuberculosis (TB) in mice, B lymphocytes form follicle-like structures, (2) these structures peak at weeks 7 to 8 post-infection (p.i.) in the lungs of infected mice and (3) lung B cells constitutively express major histocompatibility complex II molecules and present mycobacterial antigents to immune CD4 T cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of B-cells in the pathogenesis of tuberculosis, and the mechanisms of their involvement in the formation of granulomas.
the dynamics of B cell follicle formation in tuberculous lungs and the functional activity of B cells residing in the granuloma microenvironment.
B-cell response to TB infection in the lung, and its contribution to the pathology of this disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
B cells play an important but not decisive role in TB pathogenesis and immunity.
the B cells in the lungs during TB infection are not involved in anti-TB immunity, but rather in the pathology of the infection.
B cell follicles in the lung of TB-infected mice are a hallmark of the disease and have no apparent beneficial effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

lung B cells in tuberculosis are activated by the local microenvironment to produce IL-6 and other proinflammatory cytokines, and are capable to present antigen to T cells, but they are not capable to produce antibodies with specificity to mycobacterial antigents.
lung B cells are a part of the lung granuloma and have the ability to produce proinflammatory cytokines, however, their role in the anti-TB immune response in the lung is not clear.
lung B cells are activated by mycobacteria and produce cytokines that promote granuloma formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lung B cell response to mycobacteria is different from the systemic response and that lung B cells are not a major source of anti-mycobacterial antibodies.
lung B cell response to TB is not protective, and may even have a negative impact.
the lung is a major site of anti-TB humoral immunity, and the B cell response in this organ is different from the systemic one.
